adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The town of Harlow Bridge holds its summer music festival on the first weekend of August, when the river is low enough for the meadow beside the old mill to be used for the main stage. Preparations begin in March. Volunteers repaint the bandstand, mend the canvas awnings, and write to every shop on the high street asking for raffle prizes. The organising committee meets in the back room of the White Hart, and the minutes of those meetings are, by general agreement, the least exciting documents produced anywhere in the county.

This year the programme ran from Friday evening to Sunday afternoon. A brass band from the coast opened proceedings with a set of marches that the older members of the audience knew by heart. A choir of schoolchildren followed, and the applause lasted longer than the performance. Between sets, people queued for tea and sausages, and the queue for the sausages was, predictably, twice as long.

Saturday brought the rain that the committee had feared since March. The canvas awnings held, mostly. A folk trio played through a failing amplifier, and the audience, huddled under umbrellas, pretended not to notice. By four o'clock the meadow had become a shallow lake of mud, and the stewards handed out bin bags for people to sit on. Nobody left. The trio played an encore, and a man near the front began to dance, badly, alone, until two children joined him and then a dozen more.

The raffle raised eighty pounds, most of it from a single visitor who bought a strip of tickets for each of his grandchildren and then forgot to collect the prize. The prize, a hamper of local cheese and jam, was eventually given to the woman who had sold the tickets. She protested, briefly, and then accepted it with good grace.

Parking was the usual difficulty. The field behind the pub took forty cars, and by Saturday lunchtime there were fifty-two, arranged in rows that only made sense to the man directing them. He wore an orange jacket and a hat that had once belonged to his father, and he waved each car into a space with the solemnity of a man guiding aeroplanes.

Sunday was clear and cold. The final concert was given over to chamber music in the mill itself, where the acoustics are better than anyone expects. The programme listed a piano quartet and a string serenade. The cellist, Katarzyna Wojciechowska, had driven up from London that morning and arrived with ten minutes to spare, which the committee treated as a triumph of logistics. She played the slow movement of the quartet with her eyes closed, and for four minutes the mill was completely silent except for the water outside.

Afterwards the committee counted the takings in the back room of the White Hart. They had made enough to repair the roof of the bandstand and, if the estimate held, to replace the amplifier. Someone suggested that next year they should book the cellist again, and someone else wrote it down. The minutes of that meeting, when they were typed up the following week, ran to a single paragraph.
